title: Irenaeus, Tertullian, Cyprian, Augustine: second commandment and Decalogue still bind Christians (Sabbath flesh excepted)
source_text: XXIV. Id videre est apud Irenaeum libr. 4. cap. 34. Decalogi, inquit, verba omnibus similiter Dominus locutus est: ideo permanent apud nos, extensionem & augmentum, sed non dissolutionem accipientia per carnalem ejus adventum. Tertullianus vero, libro de idololatria cap. 4. loquitur de lege quae vetat fieri ullam similitudinem eorum quae sunt in coelo, vel in terra, tanquam a Deo toti mundo lata. Lex divina, inquit, proclamat, Ne feceritis idolum. Et conjungens, Neque similitudinem eorum quae in coelo sunt, & quae in terra, & quae in mari. Toto mundo ejusmodi artibus interdixit. Et capite sequenti, Si, inquit, eundem Deum observas, cum eo, scilicet, qui est legis author, babes legem ejus, Ne feceris similitudinem. Et similiter Cyprianus, verba haec secundi praecepti, Non facies tibi cujusquam similitudinem, tanquam ad Christianos pertinentia refert, lib. 3. ad Quirinum cap. 59. Praesertim vero Augustinus disertis verbis affirmat ad nos pertinere maxime Decalogum, qui duabus illis lapideis tabulis continetur, excepta sabbati observatione carnali. Contra duas Epistolas Pelagianorum lib. 3. cap. 4.
pass_a_gloss: That is to be seen in Irenaeus book 4, chapter 34. The words of the Decalogue, he says, the Lord has spoken similarly to all: therefore they remain among us, receiving extension and increase, but not dissolution, through his carnal advent. But Tertullian, in the book on idolatry chapter 4, speaks of the law which forbids any likeness of those things which are in heaven, or on earth, to be made, as laid down by God for the whole world. The divine law, he says, proclaims, Ye shall not make an idol. And joining, Nor the likeness of those things which are in heaven, and which are on earth, and which are in the sea. He has interdicted arts of that kind to the whole world. And in the following chapter, If, he says, you observe the same God, with him, namely, who is the author of the law, you have his law, Thou shalt not make a likeness. And likewise Cyprian refers these words of the second commandment, Thou shalt not make for thyself the likeness of any, as pertaining to Christians, book 3 to Quirinus chapter 59. But especially Augustine affirms in express words that the Decalogue pertains to us maximally, which is contained in those two stone tables, excepting the carnal observation of the sabbath. Against two Epistles of the Pelagians book 3, chapter 4.
pass_b_english: Irenaeus: Decalogue words remain, extended not dissolved by the Incarnation.
Tertullian universalizes the ban on likeness-making; Cyprian applies the second commandment to Christians; Augustine keeps the whole Decalogue except carnal Sabbath.

lemmas.gloss: He has interdicted ... to the whole world
